selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: High semantic compression
selected.instruction: Score 10 when every word contributes a distinct layer of premise, reference, or punchline and the entry remains immediately interpretable; score 0 when brevity produces genericness or incompleteness.
selected.rationale: The compact shirt concepts in R06, R32, and R39 carry substantial comic implication in very few words.

selected.name: Prompt-Form Fusion
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the required form actively creates the joke’s timing, meaning, or payoff; score 0 when the same joke would work unchanged in any format.
selected.rationale: R08, R47, and R53 use limerick structure to carry setup into punch. R55 suggests why rhyme alone is insufficient without form reinforcing the comic mechanism.

selected.name: Entry's own form embodies or enacts its content
selected.instruction: Score whether the entry's linguistic form demonstrates or contradicts the very property it names or describes (self-reference), rather than merely describing that property from outside. 10 = the form is inseparable from the content -- the entry could not make its point without exhibiting the property itself. 0 = form and content are unrelated; the entry simply states something without enacting it.
selected.rationale: R51 ("Monosyllabic" as an oxymoron because the word itself has five syllables) is a clean self-demonstrating joke and is dense_high_card_low; R35 ("The High School SAT Preperation Kit", where "Preperation" is itself misspelled) similarly enacts its own point and is card_high_dense_low -- self-demonstration cuts across the disagreement in both directions.
member_names: Entry enacts its own point rather than asserting it
Entry's own form embodies or enacts its content

selected.name: Reference as comic machinery
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a required famous person or institution actively generates the joke through a distinctive association; score 0 when the reference is only an attached name-drop.
selected.rationale: The identities in R04 and R17 make the lines work, whereas a merely present celebrity or institution would satisfy the prompt without adding much.

selected.name: Stable false logic
selected.instruction: Score 10 when an apparently sensible statement survives an initial reading but collapses under a precise, internally coherent contradiction; score 0 when it is simply nonsensical or conventionally paradoxical.
selected.rationale: R46, R48, R49, and R58 construct believable reasoning whose flaw becomes funnier on inspection.

selected.name: Adverbial Semantic Snap
selected.instruction: Score 10 when a quoted statement and its manner adverb are both natural yet jointly expose a second meaning; score 0 when the adverb is merely decorative.
selected.rationale: R09, R21, and R51 pair denials with adverbs that undercut or reframe them. R44 and R56 show the same mechanism, beyond simply mentioning a famous person.

selected.name: Construction Beyond Shock
selected.instruction: Score 10 when crude, dark, or offensive material is transformed by exact wordplay, irony, or targeting; score 0 when shock or offensiveness is the only substantial mechanism.
selected.rationale: R22, R26, and R39 invoke death, slurs, or danger, while R55 uses crude imagery. This criterion distinguishes mechanically precise transgression from material that relies mainly on provocation.
member_names: Transgression is carried by construction, not supplied raw

selected.name: Engages the prompt's specific conceit, not just its category
selected.instruction: Read the qualifying language in the prompt - the adjective, the twist, the stated purpose - and score whether the entry answers that qualifier or only the broad category. Score 10 when the entry could only have been written for this exact prompt because it turns on the qualifier itself. Score 5 when the entry fits the category well and glances at the qualifier. Score 0 when the entry satisfies the category generically and would serve equally well as a submission to a differently-qualified version of the same prompt.
selected.rationale: The T-shirt prompt asks for the transcendent indignity of this contest, and R48, R03 and R05 all target self-humiliation specifically (dense .84-.95, card .12-.26). R55 ('It Had to Be You' for Adam and Eve) turns exactly on the 'should not play' qualifier at dense .85 / card .21. Meanwhile R10 ('Lesser Hyattsville') and R47 ('Palookaville, USA') are card .78-.98 against dense .25-.28 and are generic bad names not fitted to any particular category. A bank scoring 'responds to the prompt' at category granularity credits both.
member_names: Delivers the literal output form the prompt demands
Engages the prompt's specific conceit, not just its category

selected.name: Exact two-reading wordplay
selected.instruction: Score 10 when the altered word or phrase supports two clear, related readings and the change is minimal but consequential; score 0 when it is merely a misspelling, loose homophone, or one-step pun.
selected.rationale: The card-favored puns in R13, R15, and R24 suggest that simple word substitution can be over-credited, unlike the more structurally layered collision in R14.

selected.name: Self-contained logical or lexical riddle operation
selected.instruction: Score how cleanly the entry works as a self-contained riddle -- a precise logical inversion, category trick, or lexical operation performed on the prompt's own constraint -- that resolves without requiring any outside cultural knowledge. 10 = an elegant, symmetric logical or lexical twist a reader can verify using only the prompt and the entry text. 0 = no logical or lexical operation is present; the entry is a flat statement or requires outside facts to make sense.
selected.rationale: R17 ("What is the opposite of a head count?") is a clean self-contained inversion of the prompt's own premise, and R12 (identifying the item that "does not belong" because the other two share the letter "M") substitutes a lexical trick for the expected semantic category; both are card_high_dense_low, suggesting the scorecard rewards this closed-form riddle logic more than the dense model does.
member_names: Self-contained logical or lexical riddle operation

selected.name: Entry breaks frame to comment on itself or the contest
selected.instruction: Score how much the entry steps outside its ostensible task to comment on its own quality, on the contest, or on the act of judging or submitting, with that self-aware commentary itself constituting the joke. 10 = the entry is substantially or entirely meta-commentary that succeeds as humor about the contest or joke-making process itself. 0 = the entry stays entirely within the fiction of the prompt with no acknowledgment of the contest or of itself as an entry.
selected.rationale: R25 (explaining, in-character as a New Yorker cartoon editor, that an unfunny cartoon's caption is secretly an anagram for "Little Weak") and R36 (a full first-person essay about the experience of entering the Style Invitational itself) both use frame-breaking self-awareness as their core device and are card_high_dense_low.
member_names: Entry breaks frame to comment on itself or the contest

selected.name: Entry text is complete, not cut off mid-thought
selected.instruction: Score whether the entry reads as a self-contained, finished unit of text versus appearing to break off before a clause, sentence, or thought is finished. 10 = entry is unambiguously complete as given. 0 = entry visibly stops mid-sentence or mid-clause with no closing punctuation resolving the thought.
selected.rationale: R28 ("(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling") is dense_high_card_low and reads as cut off mid-sentence, while R24 ("Something That Will Never Become") is card_high_dense_low and is similarly truncated; textual completeness shows up on both sides of the disagreement and deserves direct scoring rather than an assumption that truncation always signals corpus noise.
member_names: Entry text is complete, not cut off mid-thought

selected.name: Full multi-line structural completion, not a fragment
selected.instruction: Score the degree to which the entry executes a COMPLETE multi-part form (e.g. all five limerick lines with consistent meter and AABBA rhyme, or a full narrative arc) rather than delivering only a title, a fragment, or a single clever line. 10 = every structural unit the invoked form requires is present and internally consistent. 0 = entry is a title only, a sentence fragment, or otherwise stops well short of the form it invokes.
selected.rationale: R20 and R23 are complete, technically executed limericks (dense_high_card_low), while R04 ("The Secret Agent's Lament") is only a title with no poem body yet is also dense_high_card_low -- separating the two lets us test whether full-form execution specifically is under-credited by the scorecard bank.
member_names: Full multi-line structural completion, not a fragment

selected.name: Non-Arbitrary Concept Bridge
selected.instruction: Score 10 when disparate ideas are joined by one discoverable, exact relationship; score 0 when they are merely placed together for surreal or random effect.
selected.rationale: R17 and R23 juxtapose disparate material with relatively weak connecting logic. R43 and R45 show stronger cases where the unusual elements are tied by one precise, intelligible relation.

selected.name: In-text irregularity reads as clearly intentional, not noise
selected.instruction: Score how unambiguously a spelling or grammar irregularity in the entry is signaled as INTENTIONAL and load-bearing for the joke, as opposed to being indistinguishable from an accidental typo or a transcription/formatting artifact. 10 = impossible to read the irregularity as anything but a deliberate joke given the surrounding context. 0 = the irregularity could easily be mistaken for noise, with nothing signaling it is meant as humor.
selected.rationale: R35's "Preperation" typo is legible as intentional once the SAT-prep irony is noticed (card_high_dense_low); by contrast R28's abrupt cutoff ("...This is a beguiling") is much harder to read confidently as a deliberate device rather than a corpus artifact (dense_high_card_low) -- distinguishing signaled-intentional wordplay from ambiguous noise is a judgment a rigid criterion bank might not make reliably.
member_names: In-text irregularity reads as clearly intentional, not noise

selected.name: Title-only compression
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry is a very short title, slogan, label, or noun phrase without explanation or elaboration. Do not judge whether the brevity is clever or appropriate.
selected.rationale: R02, R04, R10, R15, R25, R31, R51, and R55 are highly compressed one-liners. Extreme brevity may correlate with a submitter's strategy or familiarity, while concise writing can also genuinely affect quality.

selected.name: Density of early-1990s news-cycle proper nouns
selected.instruction: Score how many references to people, institutions or events that were prominent in the news of a narrow period appear in the entry. Count named public figures, current officeholders, athletes, litigants, scandals and product names. Score 0 for none, 4 for one, 7 for two, 10 for three or more; add nothing for how apt the reference is. Score topical-name density only. You must NOT judge whether the reference is funny, well chosen, or recognisable to you.
selected.rationale: R07 (Bobbitt), R25 (Buttafuoco), R27 (Hazelwood) and R58 (Ted Kennedy) are dense .851-.960 and card .272-.428; R59 (Gheorge Muresan) and R47 (Marilyn Vos Savant) carry the same kind of marker at the opposite corner, card .837 and .962 against dense .128 and .399. The density of period-specific names is set by when the contest ran, not by the entrant's skill, and it gives a text model a strong date and container cue.
member_names: Density of dated, real-world scandal or news proper nouns
Density of early-1990s news-cycle proper nouns
selected.upstream_parent: the publication date of the contest and the news cycle running that week
upstream_parent_all_members: temporal proximity between the entry's submission and a salient news cycle (a submission-timing/zeitgeist effect on the receiving audience's recognition and enjoyment), and possible reader/editor recency bias
the publication date of the contest and the news cycle running that week

selected.name: Submission-template residue
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of headings, labels, prompt restatements, answer markers, quote numbers, colons, or unfinished-looking scaffolding. Do not judge whether the formatting is appropriate.
selected.rationale: R22, R26, R42, R50, R56, and R60 retain labels such as “Quote,” “Answer,” or category scaffolding. These traces may reflect preparation or copy-editing processes rather than humor.

selected.name: Truncation residue: fragment, dangling colon, mid-sentence stop
selected.instruction: Score how much the text reads as a cut-off or partial capture rather than a complete submission. Score 10 when it stops mid-sentence or mid-phrase, ends on a bare colon or dash, or consists solely of a heading, a title, a category label, a lead-in, or a quoted stimulus with no response attached. Score 5 when it is grammatically complete but conspicuously missing a component the prompt names. Score 0 when the text is a whole, self-contained submission. Score the extent of the truncation fingerprint only. You must NOT judge whether the fragment is nonetheless witty.
selected.rationale: R38 stops mid-sentence at 'This is a beguiling' and is the single highest dense item in the slice at dense .999; R21 ('Something That Will Never Become') stops mid-phrase; R32 ends on a bare '--'; R37 and R29 end on bare colons; R52 is a title alone; R36 and R40 are quoted stimuli with no continuation. These fragments land at both extremes of the disagreement, which is the signature of a scraping artifact rather than of writing quality: nothing about the entrant produced the cut.
member_names: Entry text ends abruptly without closing punctuation or sense
Truncation residue: fragment, dangling colon, mid-sentence stop
selected.upstream_parent: corpus extraction and segmentation - how the archived contest column was split into per-entry records
upstream_parent_all_members: corpus extraction and segmentation - how the archived contest column was split into per-entry records
how the item was extracted or paginated from the original print column into this corpus (a mining/parsing artifact), independent of anything the entrant wrote

selected.name: Convergent attribution: multiple independent entrants credited
selected.instruction: Score the extent to which the attribution indicates that more than one person submitted this same item independently. Score 0 when a single entrant or none is named, 5 when two names appear or the word 'also' introduces a second submitter, and 10 when three or more separate name-and-city entries are listed. Score the visible multiplicity of credited submitters only. You must NOT infer or judge anything about the entry's merit from how many people are credited.
selected.rationale: R04 lists three submitters (card .944 / dense .405), R35 uses the explicit 'also' construction, and R44 and R30 each list two. Convergence is a fingerprint of an idea's availability, which is a property of the prompt-plus-population rather than of the writing. Tagged mixed because a phrase several sharp entrants independently found may also be genuinely apt, so the parent plausibly causes real quality as well as this fingerprint.
member_names: Convergent attribution: multiple independent entrants credited
Multiple independently credited submitters for one entry
selected.upstream_parent: independent co-discovery - how many entrants arrived at the same idea, i.e. how obvious the idea was given the prompt
upstream_parent_all_members: how obvious or independently-discoverable the underlying idea was to the broader entrant pool, and the editors' practice of crediting all independent duplicates rather than picking one
independent co-discovery - how many entrants arrived at the same idea, i.e. how obvious the idea was given the prompt

selected.name: Trailing parenthetical attribution block present and long
selected.instruction: Score how much trailing attribution apparatus appears at the end of the entry: a parenthetical containing personal names and place names. Score 0 when there is none, 3 when a single name-and-city appears, 6 when a name-and-city plus a second locality or an out-of-state marker appears, and 10 when the parenthetical runs to multiple full names with cities. Score only the presence and size of this block. You must NOT judge whether attribution is desirable, nor let the block's contents influence your reading of the joke itself.
selected.rationale: Attribution blocks are present in roughly half the slice and absent in the other half in a way that tracks nothing about the writing: R04 carries three full name-and-city pairs (card .944), R59 and R47 carry one each, while R54, R11, R43 and R45 carry none. The block is editorial furniture added downstream of the entrant, not part of the entry, and its presence adds tokens, proper nouns and punctuation that a text-only model can read as signal.
member_names: Trailing parenthetical attribution block present and long
selected.upstream_parent: corpus construction and archival formatting - whether the byline survived transcription into the dataset
upstream_parent_all_members: corpus construction and archival formatting - whether the byline survived transcription into the dataset
which stage or column of the newspaper's publication process an entry came from (e.g. a final printed winners list with credits vs an unattributed draft/finalist pool)

selected.name: First-obvious-reading of the prompt versus late-arriving riff
selected.instruction: MODE 3 - position fingerprint. Score how much the entry reads like the first thing a competent person would produce on reading the prompt, as opposed to something written by someone who has already exhausted the obvious takes. Score 0 for the most available response: a single stock phrase with one letter or syllable altered, a dictionary-level pairing, the canonical example of the category. Score 5 for a response requiring one non-obvious pivot. Score 10 for a response that argues with the prompt, answers a different question than the one asked, addresses the contest itself, or presupposes that the obvious takes are already used up. Score availability-of-the-idea only. You must NOT judge whether obvious or late responses are better; both ends can be excellent or terrible.
selected.rationale: The most-available responses cluster hard in card_high_dense_low: R11 ('Peace Corpse'), R23 ('Profiles in Scourge'), R50 ('Golden Reliever'), R28 ('Land Mine Retriever') and R16 (the cancan) are each the first phonetic tweak the prompt invites, at card .691-.938 against dense .109-.284. The far end - R33, which refuses the comparison task and answers on a spelling technicality (card .977), and R41, which turns the excuse prompt onto the contest itself (card .866) - reads as written by someone who had already seen the obvious takes taken. Position and timing in the entry stream are not properties of how good an entry is, but they leave this availability fingerprint in the text. Tagged mixed because entrants writing deep into their own attempt list may also be more practised writers.
member_names: Directness of entry as the most obvious reading of the prompt
First-obvious-reading of the prompt versus late-arriving riff
selected.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing - where in the week's flood of submissions, and how deep into an entrant's own list of attempts, an item was produced
upstream_parent_all_members: position in the entry stream -- whether the item was likely conceived early, before other obvious takes were used up, or arrived after many similar entries had already been submitted
position in the entry stream and submission timing - where in the week's flood of submissions, and how deep into an entrant's own list of attempts, an item was produced

selected.name: Orthographic and encoding anomalies
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent of misspellings, malformed characters, unusual transliterations, missing accents, or visibly corrupted typography. Do not judge whether the anomalies help or hurt the entry.
selected.rationale: R09 contains a malformed character, while R34 and R47 contain conspicuous spelling or transliteration irregularities. Such artifacts can predict textual handling without representing the underlying joke.

selected.name: Raw word/token length of the entry text
selected.instruction: Count or estimate the total number of words in the ENTRY text only, excluding the attribution parenthetical. Score 0 = extremely short (a title, a single phrase, under about 5 words) up to 10 = long, multi-sentence text (a full poem, paragraph, or multi-clause joke). This is a pure length measurement -- do not judge whether the length is appropriate or whether the entry is good.
selected.rationale: R44 and R54 are full four/five-line limericks (dense_high_card_low) while R02 and R25 are single short sentences (dense_low_card_high); if raw length tracks the split independent of any judged wit, it is a nuisance the discounted readout should strip out.
member_names: Raw verbosity: total word count of the entry
Raw word/token length of the entry text
selected.upstream_parent: entry format/category (some prompts structurally demand short outputs, others long ones) and possible editorial space constraints on how much text a given slot in the print column can hold
upstream_parent_all_members: entry format/category (some prompts structurally demand short outputs, others long ones) and possible editorial space constraints on how much text a given slot in the print column can hold

selected.name: Late-riff residue
selected.instruction: Score 0-10 for the extent to which the entry shows a second-order, self-referential, defensive, or residual riff that reads as reacting to already-obvious approaches. Judge only the textual signs; do not infer actual submission order or judge originality.
selected.rationale: A crowded stream or late arrival could leave this fingerprint, and the resulting reaction can sometimes affect genuine quality, so it is mixed. Self-aware or meta-presentational traces occur in R14, R41, and R46.
